docs.title: 📊 HolySheet
docs.text:
Python-first report compiler that generates beautiful, interactive dashboards — in a single line of code.

[![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/holysheet?color=3B82F6&style=flat-square)](https://pypi.org/project/holysheet) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/holysheet?color=8B5CF6&style=flat-square)](https://pypi.org/project/holysheet) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/UnicoLab/HolySheet?color=10B981&style=flat-square)](https://github.com/UnicoLab/HolySheet/blob/main/LICENSE)

docs.title: Get Started in 30 Seconds
docs.text:
pip install holysheet
my_dashboard.py
from holysheet import Report, KPI, LineChart, DataTable

report = Report(title="Q4 Business Review", theme="dark")

report.add(KPI(label="Revenue", value="$2.26M", delta="+34%", status="positive"))
report.add(KPI(label="Users", value="42,000", delta="+72%", status="positive"))
report.add(LineChart(title="Revenue Trend", data=monthly_data, x="month", y="revenue"))
report.add(DataTable(title="Top Clients", data=clients))

report.export_html("report.html")  # ← Open in any browser. Done.

That's it!

The generated HTML is fully self-contained — no server, no internet, no Node.js required. Just open it in a browser, email it, or upload it anywhere.

docs.title: Why HolySheet?
docs.text:
• Python-First

    Write dashboards in pure Python. No HTML, CSS, or JavaScript knowledge needed. Full type hints and Pydantic validation.

  • Single-File Export

    Generate a standalone .html file (~1.5 MB) with everything embedded. Share via email, Slack, S3, or Confluence.

  • 47 Block Types

    KPIs, 15 chart types (line, bar, area, pie, scatter, radar, gauge, funnel, treemap, heatmap, candlestick, sankey, waterfall, boxplot, map), tables, timelines, user cards, and more.

  • 3 Premium Themes

    Dark, Light, and Executive themes with complete design systems — colors, typography, spacing, and chart palettes.

  • Any Data Source

    Native support for Pandas DataFrames, Polars DataFrames, Python dicts, and lists. Auto-detection, zero config.

  • Powered by React

    Interactive dashboards rendered with React + ECharts under the hood. Searchable tables, responsive layouts, smooth animations.

docs.title: First Public Release
docs.text: The initial release of HolySheet — a Python-first report compiler that generates beautiful, portable, interactive React dashboards.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
• Report class — Main entry point for composing dashboards with method chaining
  • 26 block types organized into 5 categories (KPI/Metrics, Charts, Data/Content, Layout, Interactive)
  • 3 built-in themes — dark, light, executive — each with a complete design system
  • 3 export modes — Standalone HTML, folder, and JSON
  • CLI — holysheet validate, holysheet serve, holysheet version

  • Metric — Compact inline metrics for dense grids

Data & Content:

  • DataTable — Interactive, searchable, paginated data tables
  • Markdown — Rich text content with full Markdown support
  • CodeBlock — Syntax-highlighted code display
  • Image — Image display with captions
  • Alert — Callout blocks (info, success, warning, error)
  • ProgressBar — Progress indicators with custom colors

Layout:

  • Section — Grouping container with heading and description
  • Columns — Multi-column responsive grid (equal, bento, custom widths)
  • Tabs — Tabbed content panels
  • Divider — Visual separators with optional labels

Interactive:

docs.title: Data Support
docs.text:
• Pandas DataFrames — Auto-conversion via .to_dict(orient='records')
  • Polars DataFrames — Auto-conversion via .to_dicts()
  • list[dict] — Pass-through with value sanitization
  • dict[str, list] — Column-oriented to row-oriented conversion
  • Value sanitization — Automatic handling of NaN, Inf, Decimal, datetime, numpy scalars

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Pydantic v2 models for all blocks with full type safety and validation
  • JSON schema spec (v1.0.0) consumed by the React renderer
  • Pre-built React bundle — No Node.js required at runtime
  • Jinja2 templates for HTML generation
  • orjson for fast JSON serialization

  • Custom exception hierarchy (HolySheetError, DataConversionError, ExportError, etc.)
  • loguru debug logging

docs.title: Data Sources
docs.text: HolySheet auto-detects and converts data from multiple Python data formats. You never need to manually transform data — just pass it directly to any block that accepts data.

docs.title: List of Dicts
docs.text:
The most common format. Each dict is a row, keys are column names.

list_of_dicts.py
data = [
    {"month": "Jan", "revenue": 124_500, "costs": 78_200},
    {"month": "Feb", "revenue": 138_200, "costs": 82_100},
    {"month": "Mar", "revenue": 152_800, "costs": 85_600},
]

LineChart(title="Revenue Trend", data=data, x="month", y=["revenue", "costs"])

This is the internal format

Internally, HolySheet converts all data to list[dict[str, Any]]. If your data is already in this format, it passes through with minimal overhead (just value sanitization).

docs.title: Dict of Lists
docs.text:
Column-oriented format where keys are column names and values are lists.

dict_of_lists.py
data = {
    "month": ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr"],
    "revenue": [124_500, 138_200, 152_800, 149_300],
    "costs": [78_200, 82_100, 85_600, 83_900],
}

LineChart(title="Revenue Trend", data=data, x="month", y="revenue")

Uniform Length Required

All lists must have the same length. If column lengths differ, a DataConversionError is raised:

# This will raise DataConversionError
data = {
    "month": ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"],
    "revenue": [100, 200],  # Only 2 values!
}

docs.title: Value Sanitization
docs.text:
HolySheet automatically cleans values for safe JSON serialization. This happens transparently on all data formats.

Input Type Output Example None None — float NaN None float('nan') → None float Inf None float('inf') → None Decimal float Decimal("3.14") → 3.14 datetime ISO string datetime(2024, 1, 15) → "2024-01-15T00:00:00" date ISO string date(2024, 1, 15) → "2024-01-15" bytes UTF-8 string b"hello" → "hello" NumPy scalar Native Python np.float64(3.14) → 3.14 NumPy NaN None np.nan → None

Automatic NaN Handling

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"],
    "score": [95, np.nan, 87],       # NaN is auto-converted to None
    "date": pd.to_datetime(["2024-01-01", "2024-02-01", "2024-03-01"]),
})

# Just pass it — HolySheet handles the NaN and datetime conversion
DataTable(title="Scores", data=df)

docs.title: The to_records() Function
docs.text:
Under the hood, all data conversion goes through holysheet.data.to_records():

to_records_usage.py
from holysheet.data import to_records

# Convert any supported format to list[dict]
records = to_records(my_dataframe)
records = to_records(my_dict_of_lists)
records = to_records(my_list_of_dicts)

# Returns: [{"col1": val1, "col2": val2}, ...]

docs.title: Conversion Flow
docs.text:
Input Data (any format)
    │
    ├── list[dict] ──→ Clean values ──→ list[dict]
    ├── dict[str, list] ──→ Transpose ──→ Clean values ──→ list[dict]
    ├── pd.DataFrame ──→ .to_dict("records") ──→ Clean values ──→ list[dict]
    └── pl.DataFrame ──→ .to_dicts() ──→ Clean values ──→ list[dict]

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
If data cannot be converted, a DataConversionError is raised:

from holysheet.exceptions import DataConversionError

try:
    records = to_records("not valid data")
except DataConversionError as e:
    print(e.message)      # "Unsupported data type: str"
    print(e.source_type)  # "str"

docs.title: Mixing Data Sources
docs.text:
You can use different data formats across blocks in the same report:

mixed_data.py
import pandas as pd

# Some data as dicts
kpi_data = {"revenue": 2_260_000, "users": 42_000}

# Chart data from pandas
chart_df = pd.read_csv("monthly_revenue.csv")

# Table data as list of dicts
customers = [
    {"name": "Acme Corp", "mrr": "$12,400"},
    {"name": "GlobalTech", "mrr": "$9,800"},
]

report = Report(title="Mixed Sources", theme="dark")
report.add(KPI(label="Revenue", value=f"${kpi_data['revenue']:,.0f}"))
report.add(LineChart(title="Trend", data=chart_df, x="month", y="revenue"))
report.add(DataTable(title="Top Customers", data=customers))

docs.title: Large DataFrames
docs.text:
Performance Note

All data is embedded in the HTML file as JSON. Very large datasets (100K+ rows) will increase file size and may impact browser performance. Consider:

  • Aggregating data before passing to charts
  • Limiting DataTable rows to a reasonable size
  • Using paginated=True (default) for large tables

docs.title: Data is Serialized at Export Time
docs.text:
Data conversion happens when you call export_html(), export_json(), or export_folder() — not when you create the block. This means you can modify your DataFrames after adding them to blocks:

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [10, 20, 30]})
chart = LineChart(title="Chart", data=df, x="x", y="y")
report.add(chart)

# ⚠️ This modification WILL be reflected in the export
# because 'data' holds a reference to df
df["y"] = [100, 200, 300]

report.export_html("report.html")  # Uses the modified data

docs.title: Export & Deployment
docs.text: HolySheet supports three export modes and includes a CLI for validation and local serving.

docs.title: Standalone HTML
docs.text:
The recommended and default export mode. Generates a single self-contained HTML file with all CSS, JavaScript, and data embedded inline.

export_html.py
report.export_html("report.html")

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text: Property Value File size ~1.5 MB (mostly React + ECharts bundles) Dependencies None — fully self-contained Offline support  Yes Server required  No

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Reads the prebuilt React bundle (app.js) and styles (app.css) from the package
  2. Serializes your report to a JSON specification
  3. Renders everything into a Jinja2 HTML template with inline <script> and <style> tags
  4. Writes a single .html file

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
html_export_full.py
from holysheet import Report, KPI, LineChart

report = Report(title="Q4 Review", theme="dark")
report.add(KPI(label="Revenue", value="$2.26M", delta="+34%", status="positive"))
report.add(LineChart(title="Trend", data=data, x="month", y="revenue"))

# Export to current directory
path = report.export_html("report.html")
print(f"Written to: {path}")

# Export to a subdirectory (created automatically)
path = report.export_html("output/reports/q4_review.html")

Opening in Browser

import webbrowser
path = report.export_html("report.html")
webbrowser.open(f"file://{path}")

├── report.json         ← Dashboard specification
├── spec-loader.js      ← Auto-generated loader script
└── assets/
    ├── app.js          ← React application bundle
    └── app.css         ← Stylesheet

JSON Export

docs.title: Serve Locally
docs.text:
Start a local HTTP server and open the report in your default browser:

holysheet serve report.json

Options:

Flag Default Description --port, -p 8765 Port to serve on --no-open False Don't auto-open browser 
# Custom port
holysheet serve report.json --port 3000

# Don't open browser automatically
holysheet serve report.json --no-open

How Serve Works

The serve command:

  1. Reads and validates the JSON spec
  2. Exports to a temporary folder
  3. Starts a Python HTTP server
  4. Opens the browser (unless --no-open)
  5. Cleans up the temp folder on exit

docs.title: Export Tips
docs.text:
File Size

Standalone HTML files are ~1.5 MB regardless of data size (the bulk is the React + ECharts bundle). Adding more data increases the size proportionally — a report with 10,000 table rows might be ~2–3 MB.

Path Handling

All export methods accept str or pathlib.Path and automatically create parent directories:

from pathlib import Path

report.export_html(Path("output") / "reports" / "q4.html")
# Creates output/reports/ if it doesn't exist

Renderer Assets

If you see a RendererAssetError, it means the prebuilt React bundle is missing. This typically happens in development. Run:

make frontend-build

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Welcome to HolySheet! This guide will take you from zero to a fully interactive dashboard in under 5 minutes.

docs.title: Basic Install

PandasPolarsEverything

pip install holysheet[polars]

pip install holysheet[all]

Requirements

  • Python 3.11+

  • No frontend build step
  • No running server

Core dependencies (installed automatically): pydantic v2 · jinja2 · orjson · loguru · click

docs.title: Understanding the Architecture
docs.text:
HolySheet operates in two distinct phases:

Python API  →  Pydantic v2 Schema  →  JSON Spec  →  React Renderer  →  HTML Dashboard

docs.title: Build Time (Python — your machine)
docs.text:
1. Define blocks using the Python API (KPI, LineChart, etc.)
  2. Validate everything with Pydantic v2 models — catch errors early
  3. Generate a versioned JSON dashboard specification
  4. Inject the spec into a prebuilt React application
  5. Export a self-contained HTML file via Jinja2 templates

docs.title: Runtime (Browser — any machine)
docs.text:
1. Browser opens the HTML file (no server needed)
  2. React reads the embedded dashboard spec from <script id="report-data">
  3. Renders each block through a component registry (type → React component)
  4. Charts become interactive via Apache ECharts
  5. Tables support real-time search and pagination

Key Insight

The React app is prebuilt and bundled inside the Python package. End users never need Node.js, npm, or any frontend tooling. The magic happens at pip install time.

docs.title: How Blocks Work
docs.text:
Every block in HolySheet is a Pydantic v2 model with a type discriminator field:

from holysheet.blocks import KPI

kpi = KPI(label="Revenue", value="$1.2M", delta="+12%", status="positive")

# Each block serializes to a dict for the React renderer:
print(kpi.to_props())
# {'label': 'Revenue', 'value': '$1.2M', 'delta': '+12%', ...}

The Report class manages a list of blocks and assigns sequential IDs (block_001, block_002, …) for deterministic output.

docs.title: Export Formats
docs.text: HolySheet supports three export modes:

docs.title: Standalone HTML (Recommended)
docs.text:
report.export_html("report.html")

Generates a single self-contained HTML file (~1.5 MB) with embedded React, CSS, and data. Zero external dependencies.

Best for

Email attachments, Slack sharing, embedding in Confluence or Notion, offline viewing.

docs.title: Folder Export
docs.text:
report.export_folder("dist/")

Generates a deployable folder structure:

dist/
├── index.html          ← Entry point
├── report.json         ← Dashboard spec
├── spec-loader.js      ← Auto-generated loader
└── assets/
    ├── app.js          ← React bundle
    └── app.css         ← Styles

Best for

Hosting on a web server, S3, CDN, or GitHub Pages.

docs.title: JSON Export
docs.text:
report.export_json("report.json")

Exports just the dashboard specification as JSON.

Best for

Debugging, version control, feeding into external rendering pipelines, programmatic manipulation.

docs.title: How Blocks Work
docs.text:
Every block inherits from Block — a Pydantic v2 BaseModel with a type discriminator:

Basic block usage
from holysheet import Report, KPI, LineChart

report = Report(title="Dashboard", theme="dark")

# Just instantiate and add
report.add(KPI(label="Revenue", value="$1.2M", delta="+12%", status="positive"))
report.add(LineChart(title="Trend", data=my_data, x="date", y="revenue"))  # (1)!

report.export_html("dashboard.html")

Method Chaining

report.add() returns self, so you can chain calls:

report.add(KPI(label="A", value=1)).add(KPI(label="B", value=2))

docs.title: Charts
docs.text: HolySheet includes 18 chart types powered by Apache ECharts, providing rich interactive visualizations with tooltips, legends, and responsive sizing.

docs.title: Common Props
docs.text:
All chart blocks share these common props:

Prop Type Default Description title str required Chart title displayed above the chart data Any None Tabular data (list of dicts, dict of lists, pandas/polars DataFrame) height int 360 Chart height in pixels

Data Formats

All chart data props accept any of the supported data formats — lists of dicts, dict of lists, pandas DataFrames, or polars DataFrames. Data is automatically converted to records internally.

docs.text:

    y=["revenue", "costs", "profit"],  # Multiple Y columns
    height=420,
)

Multi-Series Pattern

When y is a list, each column becomes its own line with a legend entry. This works the same way for AreaChart and BarChart.

docs.title: DAGChart
docs.text: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) for visualizing workflows, dependency trees, and pipeline architectures.

docs.title: Props
docs.text:
Prop Type Default Description title str required Chart title nodes list[dict] [] List of node dicts with id, label, and optional color, icon edges list[dict] [] List of edge dicts with from, to, and optional label height int 400 Chart height in pixels layout "force" \| "circular" "force" Graph layout algorithm

Data Pipeline

dag_example.py
from holysheet import DAGChart

DAGChart(
    title="ML Pipeline",
    nodes=[
        {"id": "ingest", "label": "Data Ingestion"},
        {"id": "clean", "label": "Cleaning"},
        {"id": "features", "label": "Feature Engineering"},
        {"id": "train", "label": "Model Training"},
        {"id": "eval", "label": "Evaluation"},
        {"id": "deploy", "label": "Deployment"},
    ],
    edges=[
        {"from": "ingest", "to": "clean"},
        {"from": "clean", "to": "features"},
        {"from": "features", "to": "train"},
        {"from": "train", "to": "eval"},
        {"from": "eval", "to": "deploy"},
        {"from": "eval", "to": "train", "label": "retrain"},
    ],
    layout="force",
)

docs.title: Layout Options
docs.text:
Force (default)Circular

Physics-based force-directed layout — nodes repel each other and edges act as springs. Best for general-purpose graphs.

DAGChart(title="Graph", nodes=nodes, edges=edges, layout="force")

Nodes arranged in a circle. Best for small graphs where you want to emphasize connectivity.

DAGChart(title="Graph", nodes=nodes, edges=edges, layout="circular")

DAGChart vs SankeyChart

Use DAGChart when you want to show structural relationships (dependencies, workflows). Use SankeyChart when you want to show flow quantities (revenue attribution, energy transfers).

docs.title: With Pandas
docs.text:
correlation_pandas.py
import pandas as pd
from holysheet import CorrelationMatrix

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "revenue": [100, 200, 150, 300, 250],
    "users": [1000, 2000, 1500, 3000, 2500],
    "nps": [72, 78, 75, 82, 80],
    "churn": [5.2, 4.1, 4.8, 3.2, 3.8],
})

corr = df.corr()

CorrelationMatrix(
    title="Metric Correlations",
    labels=corr.columns.tolist(),
    matrix=corr.values.tolist(),
)

Pre-computed Matrix

Unlike most chart blocks, CorrelationMatrix does not accept raw data. You need to pre-compute the correlation matrix (e.g. via df.corr() in pandas).

For charts that support y as a list (LineChart, AreaChart, BarChart), each column in the list becomes its own series in the chart:

docs.title: Data Format Quick Reference
docs.text:
Chart X/Category Y/Value Optional LineChart x (str) y (str or list) series AreaChart x (str) y (str or list) series BarChart x (str) y (str or list) series PieChart name (str) value (str) — ScatterChart x (str) y (str) size, category RadarChart indicators (list) values in data — GaugeChart — value (number) thresholds FunnelChart name (str) value (str) — TreemapChart name (str) value (str) category HeatmapChart x, y (str) value (str) — CandlestickChart x (str) open, close, low, high — SankeyChart nodes (list) links (list) — WaterfallChart category (str) value (str) — BoxPlotChart categories (list) data (nested lists) — MapChart lat, lng (str) value (str) name GanttChart — tasks (list) height DAGChart nodes (list) edges (list) layout CorrelationMatrix labels (list) matrix (nested lists) —

Data Required

Most charts require data to be provided. If data is None, the chart will render with no data points. The exceptions are GaugeChart (uses a direct value prop), SankeyChart (uses nodes/links), BoxPlotChart (uses nested lists), GanttChart (uses tasks), DAGChart (uses nodes/edges), and CorrelationMatrix (uses matrix/labels).

docs.text:
Generate a DataProfile directly from a pandas DataFrame:

import pandas as pd
from holysheet import DataProfile

df = pd.read_csv("customers.csv")

# Build column profiles from pandas describe
profiles = []
for col in df.columns:
    profile = {
        "name": col,
        "dtype": str(df[col].dtype),
        "count": int(df[col].count()),
        "null_count": int(df[col].isna().sum()),
        "null_pct": round(df[col].isna().mean() * 100, 2),
        "unique": int(df[col].nunique()),
    }
    if df[col].dtype in ("float64", "int64"):
        profile["mean"] = round(df[col].mean(), 2)
        profile["std"] = round(df[col].std(), 2)
        profile["min"] = round(df[col].min(), 2)
        profile["max"] = round(df[col].max(), 2)
    else:
        profile["top"] = str(df[col].mode().iloc[0]) if len(df[col].mode()) > 0 else None
        profile["freq"] = int(df[col].value_counts().iloc[0]) if len(df[col]) > 0 else None
    profiles.append(profile)

DataProfile(title=f"Profile: {df.shape[0]} rows × {df.shape[1]} cols", columns=profiles)

docs.title: How Interactive State Works
docs.text: Interactive blocks in HolySheet render as functional UI controls in the browser. Here's how they work:

docs.title: Current Behavior
docs.text:
1. Visual Controls — Sliders, number inputs, and toggles render as fully interactive React components
  2. Local State — Each control maintains its own local state in the browser
  3. Display Only — Currently, changing a control's value does not automatically filter or update other blocks in the dashboard

Interactive Blocks Are Visual

In the current version (v0.3.0), interactive blocks serve as visual input elements. They display and respond to user interaction within the dashboard but do not yet trigger cross-block reactivity.

docs.title: Future Roadmap
docs.text:
Future versions of HolySheet plan to introduce:

  • Cross-block reactivity — Slider changes filtering chart data in real-time
  • Event callbacks — Python-defined logic for control interactions
  • Linked controls — Multiple controls driving shared state
  • Dashboard filters — Global filter bar with interactive controls

Use Case: Presentation Dashboards

Interactive blocks are already useful in presentation contexts — for example, a slider showing different scenarios, or toggles indicating which options are selected. They add polish and interactivity even without cross-block reactivity.

docs.title: Control Panel Pattern
docs.text:
A common pattern is grouping interactive controls in a "control panel" section at the top of the dashboard:

control_panel.py
from holysheet import (
    Report, Section, Columns,
    Slider, NumberInput, Toggle, Divider,
    KPI, LineChart,
)

report = Report(title="Interactive Dashboard", theme="dark")

# Control panel
report.add(Section(
    title="Dashboard Controls",
    description="Adjust parameters to explore the data",
    children=[
        Columns(children=[
            Slider(label="Time Range", min=2020, max=2026, default_value=[2023, 2026]),
            NumberInput(label="Target Revenue", min=0, max=10_000_000,
                       step=100_000, default_value=2_000_000, unit="$"),
            Toggle(label="Show Forecasts", default_value=True),
        ]),
    ],
))

report.add(Divider())

# Dashboard content
report.add(KPI(label="Revenue", value="$4.64M", delta="+23%", status="positive"))
report.add(LineChart(title="Revenue Trend", data=data, x="month", y="revenue"))

report.export_html("interactive_dashboard.html")

docs.text: KPI and Metric blocks are the headline numbers of your dashboard. They give stakeholders an instant snapshot of performance.

docs.title: KPI
docs.text: The KPI block is a full-featured key performance indicator card with support for delta values (change indicators) and semantic status colors.

docs.title: Props

    status="positive",
))

docs.title: Status Colors
docs.text:
PositiveNegativeNeutral

Formatting

The value prop accepts strings, integers, and floats. For formatted values like $2.26M, pass a pre-formatted string. For raw numbers, use int or float with a unit.

Use KPI for 3–5 hero metrics at the top of your dashboard. Use Metric inside Columns for dense secondary metric grids.

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text:
HolySheet provides a command-line interface for validating, serving, developing, linting, and comparing reports.

holysheet [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

docs.title: Global Options
docs.text: Option Description --verbose, -v Enable debug logging --help Show help and exit

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
Validate a HolySheet JSON spec file for structural correctness.

holysheet validate REPORT_JSON

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description REPORT_JSON Path to a JSON spec file

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
$ holysheet validate report.json
Validating report.json...
✓ Valid HolySheet spec
  Title:          Q4 Review
  Schema version: 1.0.0
  Theme:          dark
  Blocks:         12
  Created at:     2026-05-21T08:00:00+00:00

docs.title: serve
docs.text:
Start a local HTTP server and open the report in your default browser.

holysheet serve REPORT_JSON [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description REPORT_JSON Path to a JSON spec file

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Description --port, -p 8765 Port to serve on --no-open False Don't auto-open browser

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# Default port
$ holysheet serve report.json
Serving report.json at http://localhost:8765
Press Ctrl+C to stop.

# Custom port, no browser
$ holysheet serve report.json --port 3000 --no-open

How Serve Works

The serve command:

  1. Reads and validates the JSON spec
  2. Exports to a temporary folder
  3. Starts a Python HTTP server
  4. Opens the browser (unless --no-open)
  5. Cleans up the temp folder on exit

docs.title: version
docs.text:
Display the installed HolySheet version.

holysheet version

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
$ holysheet version
holysheet 0.4.0

docs.title: dev
docs.text:
Start a hot-reload development server that watches a Python report script for changes and automatically rebuilds and refreshes the browser.

holysheet dev SCRIPT [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description SCRIPT Path to a Python script that generates a HolySheet report

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Description --port, -p 8000 Port to serve on --no-open False Don't auto-open browser

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
$ holysheet dev my_report.py
🔥 HolySheet Dev Server
   Watching: /Users/you/project/my_report.py
   Serving:  http://localhost:8000
   Press Ctrl+C to stop.

  Building from my_report.py...
  ✓ Build #1 ready

When you save changes to my_report.py, the server automatically rebuilds:

↻ Change detected in my_report.py
  Building from my_report.py...
  ✓ Build #2 ready

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Executes the Python script via subprocess
  2. Locates the generated HTML output
  3. Injects a live-reload JavaScript snippet (polls /api/version)
  4. Serves the output via a local HTTP server
  5. Watches the script file for mtime changes (polling every 500ms)
  6. Re-executes and reloads the browser on change

Development Workflow

The dev command is the fastest way to iterate on a report. Open your script in an editor, save changes, and see the result instantly in the browser.

Script Requirements

Your script should call report.export_html() or similar. The dev server looks for HTML output in the HOLYSHEET_DEV_OUTPUT directory or the script's directory.

docs.title: lint
docs.text:
Run a linter against a HolySheet report to catch common issues, missing best practices, and potential problems.

holysheet lint SOURCE [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description SOURCE Path to a Python script (.py) or JSON spec file (.json)

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Description --strict False Treat warnings as errors (exit code 1)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
$ holysheet lint my_report.py
Linting my_report.py...

  💡 SUGGESTION [block_001]: KPI has no delta — consider adding a change indicator for context.
  ⚠️  WARNING [block_004]: Chart (line_chart) has no title — add a descriptive title for clarity.
  ✅ INFO [block_006]: DataTable has no explicit columns — columns will be auto-inferred from data.

  Found 1 warning(s), 1 suggestion(s), 1 info(s)

docs.title: Lint Rules
docs.text:
The linter checks for the following patterns:

Level Rule Description Suggestion KPI without delta KPI cards without change indicators lack context Suggestion Section > 8 children Large sections should use Tabs for organization Suggestion Consecutive same-type blocks Sequential blocks of the same type could use Columns Warning Chart without title Charts need descriptive titles for clarity Error Empty chart data Charts with empty data=[] render blank Info DataTable without columns Auto-inferred columns may be unstable Info Missing theme No explicit theme defaults to "light"

docs.title: Strict Mode
docs.text:
# Exit with error code 1 if any warnings are found
$ holysheet lint my_report.py --strict

CI Integration

Add holysheet lint --strict to your CI pipeline to catch report issues before deployment.

docs.title: diff
docs.text:
Compare two HolySheet JSON spec files and show the differences in metadata, blocks, and props.

holysheet diff FILE_A FILE_B

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description FILE_A Path to the first JSON spec file FILE_B Path to the second JSON spec file

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
$ holysheet diff report_v1.json report_v2.json
Comparing report_v1.json ↔ report_v2.json

Metadata changes:
  title: 'Q3 Review' → 'Q4 Review'
  theme: 'light' → 'dark'

Removed blocks (1):
  - kpi (block_003) "Old Metric"

Added blocks (2):
  + kpi (block_005) "New Revenue"
  + line_chart (block_006) "Revenue Trend"

Changed blocks (1):
  ~ kpi (block_001) "Revenue": props changed [delta, value]

Summary: 1 removed, 2 added, 1 changed (A: 4 blocks → B: 5 blocks)

docs.title: What It Compares
docs.text:
Category Details Metadata title, subtitle, theme, logo_url, author, report_version, footer, schema_version Removed blocks Blocks in A that are not in B (matched by block ID) Added blocks Blocks in B that are not in A Changed blocks Blocks present in both but with different type or props

Version Control

Export your reports as JSON (report.export_json("report.json")) and commit them to Git. Use holysheet diff to review changes before deploying updated reports.

docs.title: publish
docs.text:
Upload a generated HTML report to cloud storage (Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage).

holysheet publish HTML_FILE -t TARGET [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description HTML_FILE Path to the generated HTML report file

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Description --target, -t required Cloud target URL (s3://bucket/key or gs://bucket/key) --public False Make the uploaded file publicly readable

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Publish to Amazon S3
$ holysheet publish report.html -t s3://my-reports/q4/dashboard.html --public
✅ Published → https://my-reports.s3.amazonaws.com/q4/dashboard.html

# Publish to Google Cloud Storage
$ holysheet publish report.html -t gs://my-bucket/reports/q4.html
✅ Published → gs://my-bucket/reports/q4.html

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Provider SDK Credentials S3 pip install boto3 AWS credentials configured (env vars or ~/.aws/credentials) GCS pip install google-cloud-storage GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS env var

One-liner Deploy

python my_report.py && holysheet publish report.html -t s3://my-bucket/reports/latest.html --public

Add -v to any command for detailed debug output:

holysheet -v validate report.json

holysheet -v lint my_report.py

docs.title: Custom Theme API
docs.text: Create fully branded dashboards by extending any built-in theme with your own colors, fonts, and chart palette.

docs.title: Creating a Custom Theme
docs.text:
custom_theme.py
from holysheet import Report, KPI
from holysheet.themes import Theme

brand = Theme(
    name="acme",
    base="dark",                          # Extend the dark theme
    primary="#FF6B00",                     # Brand orange
    secondary="#00D4AA",                   # Teal accent
    background="#0A0A0F",                  # Deep background
    surface="#1A1A2E",                     # Card surface
    font="Satoshi",                        # Custom font
    chart_palette=["#FF6B00", "#00D4AA", "#6366F1", "#F59E0B"],
)

report = Report(title="Acme Corp Dashboard", theme=brand)
report.add(KPI(label="Revenue", value="$4.2M", delta="+18%", status="positive"))
report.export_html("acme_dashboard.html")

Only Override What You Need

The Theme class deep-copies the base theme and only overrides the properties you specify. Unset properties inherit from the base.

docs.title: Customization
docs.text:
Templates accept all Report constructor arguments via **kwargs:

template_customization.py
from holysheet.templates import SalesDashboard

report = SalesDashboard(
    data=my_data,
    theme="executive",                    # Override theme
    title="Custom Sales Report",          # Override title
    author="Data Team",                   # Pass Report kwargs
    theme_switch=True,                    # Enable feature flags
    password="s3cret",                    # Password protect
)

docs.title: Adding More Blocks
docs.text:
Since templates are Report subclasses, you can add more blocks after construction:

template_extend.py
from holysheet.templates import SalesDashboard
from holysheet import Markdown, Alert

report = SalesDashboard(data=my_data)

# Add extra blocks after the template builds
report.add(Markdown(content="## Additional Notes\n\nQ4 exceeded expectations."))
report.add(Alert(severity="info", message="Next review: Jan 15, 2027"))

report.export_html("extended_dashboard.html")

docs.title: Partial Data
docs.text:
All data keys are optional — the template gracefully skips sections when data is missing:

template_partial.py
# Only KPIs and revenue trend — no pipeline, no clients table
report = SalesDashboard(data={
    "kpis": {"revenue": "$4.2M", "deals_won": 142},
    "revenue": monthly_revenue_data,
})

Use Templates as Starting Points

Templates are great for getting a polished dashboard up quickly. For full control, compose blocks manually using the Block Types API.
